title: BitCrust: layered KV cache compression experiment for per-cohort fidelity vs memory
creator: Sofia Chen
description: Investigate a layered compression strategy ("BitCrust") for KV cache to maximize GPU memory reduction while bounding downstream quality regressions. Goal: enable aggressive on-device memory savings for long-context workloads by combining FP8 mantle, per-channel INT8, and blockwise INT4 with residual correction and a cohort-aware fidelity selector.
background: Existing KV compression probes have shown different trade-offs between memory and quality (see prior probes). BitCrust proposes a layered stack: keep recent tokens in high fidelity (FP16/FP8), mid-age tokens in INT8 per-channel with scale offsets, and cold shards in blockwise INT4 plus a lightweight residual patch. Also evaluate dynamic fallback at request-time based on request cohort (latency-sensitive vs quality-sensitive). We want to test both offline metrics and live continuous-batching traffic with realistic request mixes.
experiment_plan: 1) Implement BitCrust encoder/decoder for KV shards in the runtime (prototype documented in design doc). 2) Implement cohort classifier (small fingerprinting + TTL) that annotates requests as HIGH_QUALITY or LOW_LATENCY. 3) Run controlled A/B: baseline (no compression) vs BitCrust variant A (FP8+INT8+INT4 layered) vs variant B (FP8+INT8 with stochastic rounding but no INT4). 4) Run experiments at batch sizes representative of continuous batching (1, 8, 32) and measure latency tail, throughput, and cache eviction behavior. 5) Inject simulated drift on long dialogs and measure regression amplification. 6) Collect token-level errors, reconstruction residual, downstream ROUGE/EM/embedding cosine on evaluation prompts.
dataset_and_metrics: Datasets: long-context summarization set (Redwood-LongSum-5k), multi-turn instruction chat (Redwood-Dialog-3k), code completion traces (Redwood-Code-1k). Metrics: delta-perplexity, ROUGE-L, exact-match on code tests, embedding-cosine similarity distribution, token reconstruction MSE, 95/99th latency, throughput (tokens/sec), GPU memory footprint reduction %, and percentage of fallbacks triggered.
implementation_notes: - Per-channel INT8 uses symmetric scale stored as 16-bit per-channel scale and 8-bit zero-bias. - INT4 blockwise packing uses 64-token tiles with tile-level scale + per-tile bias. - Residual patch stores compact delta in FP8 for hot shards and in INT8 quantized deltas for cold shards. - Supporting runtime toggles for stochastic rounding and error-feedback compensation. - Added metrics hooks to export per-shard reconstruction stats to observability pipeline (console route: /kv/bitcrust).
test_runs: Run 1 (small synthetic): batch sizes [1,8]; variant A vs baseline; 10k requests each. Run 2 (traffic replay): 24h of sampled prod traffic at 10% scale in canary cluster; continuous-batching enabled. Run 3 (stress): forced eviction regimes with tight GPU memory to emulate multi-model collocation. Each run recorded seed, docker image, config flags, and PR link.
interim_results: - Memory: variant A reduced KV resident memory by 46% on average (range 38-53) across model families; variant B (no INT4) reduced by 29%. - Quality: on long-summary set variant A increased perplexity by +1.9% (median) and caused a ROUGE-L drop of 0.8 pts; variant B had +0.7% perplexity delta and 0.2 pt ROUGE-L drop. - Latency: tail (p99) increased by +6ms with variant A under batch=1 due to residual patch application; under batch=32 tail unchanged or slightly improved due to cache compactness improving GPU scheduling. - Fallbacks: cohort classifier triggered fallback to higher-fidelity tier for ~12% of HIGH_QUALITY requests and overall fallback rate for variant A was 3.4%. - Reconstruction MSE correlated strongly with downstream embedding cosine; shards with MSE>threshold caused more hallucination signals in code tests.
analysis_and_tradeoffs: - INT4 blockwise yields largest memory wins but concentrated quality regressions on rare token cohorts (numeric tables, code identifiers). - Residual patching mitigates most regressions but adds decoding work; overall cost-benefit favors keeping residuals for the top 25% hottest shards. - Cohort-aware policy reduces end-user quality regressions by routing sensitive requests off the cold INT4 tier but increases effective memory footprint. - Continuous batching interacts: larger batches amortize decoding overhead, making aggressive compression more feasible for high-throughput routes. - Operational complexity: telemetry and guardrails required (reconstruction MSE alerting, automatic rollback on quality drift).
decisions: - Proceed to refine variant A with adaptive residual budget: keep FP8 residuals for top-25% shards by access frequency, INT8 residuals for next 25%, drop for cold shards. - Implement automatic MSE-driven rollback threshold and tie to rollout traffic percentage. - Expose per-route compression profile in console with recommended presets (latency-first, balanced, quality-first).
blockers: - Need final sign-off from model team on acceptable ROUGE and embedding-cosine deltas for customer-facing models. - Storage format alignment with on-disk snapshotting for Dedicated customers (compat concerns). - A correctness bug found in stochastic rounding path causing deterministic bias for small-scale values; patch in review (PR: gh/infra/bitcrust-quant-23).
next_steps: 1) Fix stochastic rounding bias and re-run small-synthetic sweep (owner: Diego). 2) Implement adaptive residual budget scheduler and run 48h canary on Redwood-LongSum-5k (owner: Sofia). 3) Draft console UI for per-route compression knobs and rollout policy (owner: PM: Asha Patel). 4) Prepare runtime-1.20 release notes and risk matrix. 5) Schedule customer-facing technical note and migration guide for Dedicated/Private deployments.
